extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and anyone seeking an encyclopedic history of the News of the World and related journalism controversies
extracted.subtask_short: wikipedia article on News of the World
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic Wikipedia article describing the history, practices, controversies, and legal fallout of the British tabloid newspaper News of the World (1843–2011). Includes examples of journalistic techniques and ethical/legal failings associated with the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phone hacking / illegal interception of personal communications
rubrics_metrics.description: From the nineties until the newspaper's demise in 2011, reporters at the paper used private investigators to illegally gain access to hundreds of mobile phone voicemail accounts held by a variety of people of interest to the newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and consequences: Clive Goodman pleaded guilty to illegal interception and was jailed; arrests of journalists and executives followed; victims alleged as many as 7,000 people had phones hacked; disclosure that Milly Dowler's voicemail had been accessed (and potential evidence deleted) caused major public backlash leading to the paper's closure. Anti-pattern: illegal access to voicemail is both unethical and criminal and led to prosecutions, apologies, and the paper's demise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chequebook journalism / paying for stories and witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper became notorious for chequebook journalism, as it was often discovered attempting to buy stories, typically concerning private affairs and relationships, of people closely involved with figures of public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: paying key witnesses in criminal trials (e.g., the 1966 Moors murders case and the 1999 Gary Glitter trial) and paying a witness £10,000 in the Victoria Beckham 'kidnap plot' case. Anti-pattern: buying testimony or sources can produce unreliable evidence, lead to collapsed trials, and raise serious ethical and legal questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of undercover reporting, disguises and deception
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper frequently used insiders and journalists in disguise to provide video or photographic evidence and undercover reporting (e.g., Mazher Mahmood, the 'Fake Sheikh').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such techniques produced scoops but also ethical controversies and legal problems — in some cases sting operations led to trials collapsing when it was revealed that evidence was manufactured or witnesses were paid. Guidance: weigh public interest against risks of entrapment, fabrication, and legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrapment and manufacturing of stories (sting tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Undercover stings and set-ups (for example the Victoria Beckham 'kidnap plot' and other fake-sheikh operations) sometimes involved creating or encouraging wrongdoing to obtain a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: trials have collapsed when it emerged the paper had paid or manipulated witnesses; such tactics can prompt police investigations (Operation Canopus) and damage credibility. Anti-pattern: manufacturing evidence or inducing crime for a story undermines legal process and journalistic ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming-and-shaming alleged paedophiles / public identification of suspects
rubrics_metrics.description: In July 2000 the paper began a controversial campaign to name and shame alleged paedophiles—following the Sarah Payne case—which led to instances of action being taken against those suspected, including mistaken identity and vigilante actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official response: campaign labelled 'grossly irresponsible' by the chief constable of Gloucestershire. Harm noted: vandalism of an innocent paediatrician's house and confrontations with misidentified individuals. Guidance: naming suspects without due process risks serious harm, vigilantism, and legal/ethical condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corrupt sources / bribery of police officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper knowingly used private investigators and material obtained by a colleague's bribery of a police officer as the basis for articles; it knowingly used private investigators to gain stories from corrupt police officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: ties to police corruption fuelled investigations and criticism, and contributed to major scandals. Anti-pattern: reliance on bribed or corrupt officials undermines legality and credibility and can expose the outlet to legal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invasion of privacy and publishing intimate material (video / sexual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper published intimate material and video (e.g., allegations about Max Mosley involving a recorded incident) that led to invasion of privacy claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal consequences: Max Mosley won damages for invasion of privacy; publishing sexually explicit private material risks litigation and damages. Guidance: balance claimed public interest against individual privacy rights and legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and libel risk / avoiding false allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper faced many libel actions and settlements (e.g., David Beckham, Wayne Rooney, Ashley Cole, Tommy Sheridan, Barry George) arising from false or defamatory reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: damages, apologies, settlements, and long legal battles. Guidance: verify facts and sources; publishing unverified or false claims invites libel suits and severe reputational/legal costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of potential evidence and preservation obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: It was disclosed that potential evidence had been deleted from the hacked voicemail account of Milly Dowler, then missing, which intensified the scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deleting or tampering with potential evidence can worsen legal exposure and public condemnation. Guidance: journalists and organisations must preserve materials that may be relevant to investigations and respect legal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability, public apology, and cooperation with investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper 'unreservedly' apologised for phone hacking activities; executives and owners publicly stated cooperation with police investigations; senior figures were held for questioning and arrested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisational response matters: apologies, cooperation, and accountability are part of crisis management but may not avert legal or commercial consequences (withdrawal of advertising, closure). Guidance: transparent cooperation with investigations and internal accountability are necessary but follow-up reforms and legal remediation are often required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic campaign tactics and public interest vs harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper ran populist campaigns (e.g., anti-paedophile 'name and shame', rewards for information) and sensationalism focusing on celebrity scoops, gossip, and sex scandals as commercial strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While such campaigns may boost circulation and yield public interest stories, they can also produce mistakes, vigilante behaviour, ethical criticism, libel, and long-term reputational damage. Guidance: editors should weigh commercial incentives against ethical, legal and societal harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering rewards for information (practical impact and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: In December 2006 the newspaper announced a record-breaking reward of £250,000 for information leading to arrest/conviction in the Ipswich murders; the reward went unclaimed though unrelated information later led to an arrest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering rewards can encourage tips but does not guarantee results and may incentivise unreliable or opportunistic information; use with caution and verification procedures.
